lessons.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
lessons.content: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the science of making machines that can think, learn, and make decisions. AI is already everywhere: voice assistants (Siri, Google Assistant), recommendation systems (Netflix, YouTube), email spam filters, and self-driving cars. There are two types: Narrow AI (designed for one specific task, like playing chess or recognizing faces) and General AI (human-level intelligence across all tasks — this doesn't exist yet). AI works by processing large amounts of data and finding patterns that humans might miss.
examples: Spotify uses AI to recommend songs based on your listening patterns
Google Translate uses AI to translate between 100+ languages
Self-driving cars use AI to detect pedestrians, traffic signs, and other vehicles

keyTerms.artificial intelligence: Machines that can learn, reason, and make decisions from data
keyTerms.narrow AI: AI designed for one specific task (image recognition, chess, translation)
keyTerms.general AI: Hypothetical AI with human-level intelligence across all tasks — not yet achieved

quiz.question: Which is an example of narrow AI?
options: A robot that can do everything a human can
quiz.explanation: A spam filter is narrow AI — it's trained for one specific task.

quiz.question: Does General AI currently exist?
quiz.explanation: General AI (human-level across all tasks) remains a research goal, not a reality.

quiz.question: How does AI learn?
options: By processing large amounts of data and finding patterns
By being programmed with every possible answer
quiz.explanation: AI learns patterns from data — the more quality data, the better it performs.

lessons.title: History and Types of AI
lessons.content: AI began in the 1950s when Alan Turing asked 'Can machines think?' Early AI used rules written by humans (expert systems). The field had 'AI winters' when progress stalled. Modern AI took off around 2012 with deep learning — neural networks trained on massive datasets using powerful GPUs. Key types: rule-based systems (if-then logic), machine learning (learns from data), deep learning (multi-layer neural networks), and reinforcement learning (learns by trial and error, like a game-playing AI). Today's AI breakthroughs include language models (GPT, Gemma), image generators, and protein structure prediction.
examples: 1997: IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Kasparov using rule-based search
2012: Deep learning model AlexNet dramatically improved image recognition accuracy
2023: Language models like ChatGPT can write essays, code, and answer questions conversationally

keyTerms.deep learning: AI using multi-layer neural networks to learn complex patterns from data
keyTerms.neural network: A computing system inspired by the brain, made of connected nodes (neurons)
keyTerms.machine learning: AI that improves its performance by learning from data without explicit programming

quiz.question: When did the AI field begin?
quiz.explanation: AI research began in the 1950s, with Alan Turing's foundational work.

quiz.question: What powered the modern AI revolution around 2012?
options: Deep learning with large datasets and GPUs
quiz.explanation: Deep learning models trained on massive data using GPU computing drove the breakthrough.

quiz.question: How does reinforcement learning work?
options: Learning by trial and error with rewards and penalties
quiz.explanation: The AI tries actions, gets rewards for good outcomes and penalties for bad ones, learning over time.

lessons.title: AI Applications Today
lessons.content: AI is transforming every industry. Healthcare: AI analyzes medical images to detect cancer earlier than human doctors. Agriculture: drones with AI monitor crop health and predict yields. Education: AI tutors adapt to each student's learning pace (like Otic Studio!). Finance: AI detects fraudulent transactions in real-time. Transportation: self-driving vehicles and traffic optimization. Natural Language Processing (NLP) lets computers understand and generate human language — powering chatbots, translation, and voice assistants. Computer vision lets AI 'see' — facial recognition, quality inspection in factories.
examples: AI detects diabetic eye disease from retinal scans with 90%+ accuracy
Farmers use AI-powered apps to identify crop diseases from a phone photo
Banks use AI to flag suspicious transactions — blocking fraud before money is lost

keyTerms.NLP: Natural Language Processing — AI that understands and generates human language
keyTerms.computer vision: AI that can interpret and understand images and video
keyTerms.chatbot: An AI that converses with humans in natural language

quiz.question: NLP stands for:
quiz.explanation: NLP = Natural Language Processing — enabling computers to understand human language.

quiz.question: How is AI used in agriculture?
options: Monitoring crop health and predicting yields
quiz.explanation: AI analyzes drone/satellite images to monitor crop health and predict harvests.

quiz.question: Computer vision allows AI to:
quiz.explanation: Computer vision processes visual data — recognizing faces, objects, text in images.

lessons.title: Collecting and Cleaning Data
lessons.content: Data is the fuel of AI — without good data, AI can't learn. Data comes from many sources: surveys, sensors, websites, databases, social media, and IoT devices. Raw data is often messy: missing values, duplicates, typos, inconsistent formats. Data cleaning fixes these issues: fill or remove missing values, remove duplicates, standardize formats (all dates as YYYY-MM-DD), and fix typos. Data scientists spend about 80% of their time cleaning data. The quality of your AI model depends directly on the quality of your data — garbage in, garbage out.
examples: A survey has ages: 15, 16, '', 14, 999 — the blank and 999 need cleaning
Dates in mixed formats: '12/01/2024' and 'Jan 12, 2024' need standardizing
Duplicate entries: same student listed twice with slightly different spellings of their name

keyTerms.data cleaning: The process of fixing errors, inconsistencies, and missing values in data
keyTerms.dataset: A structured collection of data, often organized in rows and columns
keyTerms.missing values: Empty cells in a dataset where data should exist but doesn't

quiz.question: What percentage of a data scientist's time is spent cleaning data?
quiz.explanation: Data cleaning is the most time-consuming part — roughly 80% of the work.

quiz.question: What does 'garbage in, garbage out' mean?
options: Bad data produces bad AI results
quiz.explanation: If you train AI on low-quality data, the predictions will be low-quality too.

quiz.question: Which is a data quality issue?
quiz.explanation: Missing values are a common data quality problem that needs to be addressed.

lessons.title: Analyzing and Visualizing Data
lessons.content: Data analysis means examining data to find patterns, trends, and insights. Descriptive statistics summarize data: mean (average), median (middle), mode (most common), standard deviation (spread). Visualizations make patterns visible: bar charts compare categories, line graphs show trends over time, scatter plots show relationships between variables, pie charts show proportions. Tools: Excel/Google Sheets for basic analysis, Python (pandas, matplotlib) for advanced analysis. Always ask: What story does this data tell? What decisions can we make from it?
examples: A line graph of daily temperatures reveals a warming trend over 50 years
A scatter plot shows that students who study more hours tend to get higher grades (positive correlation)
A bar chart compares sales across 5 regions — East region is clearly the highest

keyTerms.data visualization: Representing data graphically to reveal patterns and tell stories
keyTerms.correlation: A statistical relationship between two variables (positive, negative, or none)
keyTerms.descriptive statistics: Numbers that summarize data: mean, median, mode, standard deviation

quiz.question: Which chart is best for showing trends over time?
quiz.explanation: Line graphs connect data points across time, clearly showing trends.

quiz.question: What does a positive correlation mean?
options: As one variable increases, the other also increases
As one increases, the other decreases
quiz.explanation: Positive correlation: both variables move in the same direction.

quiz.question: What tool would a beginner use for data analysis?
quiz.explanation: Spreadsheets are the most accessible tool for basic data analysis and visualization.

lessons.title: Databases and Data Storage
lessons.content: Databases organize and store large amounts of data efficiently. Relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite) store data in tables with rows and columns — like a spreadsheet but much more powerful. SQL (Structured Query Language) is used to query databases: SELECT name, age FROM students WHERE grade = 'A' retrieves specific data. NoSQL databases (MongoDB, Firebase) store data as documents or key-value pairs — more flexible for unstructured data. Cloud databases (AWS, Google Cloud) store data on remote servers accessible from anywhere. Choose based on your needs: structured data → SQL, flexible/rapid development → NoSQL.
examples: SELECT * FROM products WHERE price < 100 — finds all products under $100
A school database has tables: students, teachers, classes, grades — linked by IDs
Firebase stores a user profile as: {name: 'Alice', age: 15, interests: ['math', 'code']}

keyTerms.SQL: Structured Query Language — the standard language for querying relational databases
keyTerms.relational database: A database that stores data in tables with relationships between them
keyTerms.NoSQL: Non-relational databases that store data as documents, key-value pairs, or graphs

quiz.question: What does SQL stand for?
quiz.explanation: SQL = Structured Query Language — used to interact with relational databases.

quiz.question: When would you choose NoSQL over SQL?
options: For flexible, rapidly changing data structures
quiz.explanation: NoSQL is great when data structure varies or changes frequently.

quiz.question: What does SELECT * FROM students do?
options: Retrieves all columns and rows from the students table
quiz.explanation: SELECT * means 'select all columns' and FROM students specifies the table.

lessons.title: How Machines Learn
lessons.content: Machine learning (ML) is teaching computers to learn from data without being explicitly programmed. Instead of writing rules, you give the computer examples and it figures out the patterns. The process: collect data → clean it → split into training set and test set → choose an algorithm → train the model on training data → evaluate on test data → deploy. The model is the learned pattern — it takes new input and makes predictions. Overfitting means the model memorized training data but fails on new data (like studying answers instead of understanding concepts).
examples: Training: show the model 10,000 photos of cats and dogs with labels → it learns to distinguish them
Testing: give it 1,000 new photos it hasn't seen → measure accuracy (e.g., 95% correct)
Overfitting: model gets 99% on training data but only 60% on test data — it memorized, didn't learn

keyTerms.training data: The data used to teach the model patterns
keyTerms.test data: New data used to evaluate how well the model performs on unseen examples
keyTerms.overfitting: When a model performs well on training data but poorly on new data

quiz.question: What is the first step in machine learning?
quiz.explanation: Everything starts with data — good ML requires quality data collection and cleaning.

quiz.question: Why split data into training and test sets?
options: To evaluate if the model works on unseen data
quiz.explanation: Testing on unseen data shows if the model truly learned patterns or just memorized.

quiz.question: Overfitting means:
options: Model works on training data but fails on new data
quiz.explanation: Overfitting = memorizing instead of learning — performs well on training but poorly on real data.

lessons.title: Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning
lessons.content: Supervised learning uses labeled data — each example has an input and the correct answer. Classification predicts categories (spam or not spam, cat or dog). Regression predicts numbers (house price, temperature). Unsupervised learning finds hidden patterns in unlabeled data. Clustering groups similar items (customer segments, document topics). Dimensionality reduction simplifies complex data while keeping important information. Semi-supervised learning uses a small amount of labeled data with lots of unlabeled data — useful when labeling is expensive.
examples: Supervised classification: trained on emails labeled 'spam' or 'not spam' → predicts new emails
Supervised regression: given house features (size, location) and prices → predicts price of new house
Unsupervised clustering: given customer purchase data → discovers 3 customer groups (bargain hunters, premium, occasional)

keyTerms.supervised learning: ML using labeled data where the correct answer is provided for training
keyTerms.unsupervised learning: ML that finds patterns in unlabeled data without predefined answers
keyTerms.classification: Predicting which category something belongs to (spam/not spam, cat/dog)

quiz.question: Supervised learning requires:
quiz.explanation: Supervised = the training data includes labels (correct answers) for the model to learn from.

quiz.question: Which is a classification task?
options: Deciding if an email is spam or not
quiz.explanation: Classification assigns categories — spam/not-spam is a binary classification.

quiz.question: Clustering is an example of:
quiz.explanation: Clustering finds groups in unlabeled data — no correct answers are provided.

lessons.title: Neural Networks
lessons.content: Neural networks are computing systems loosely inspired by the human brain. They consist of layers of connected nodes (neurons): an input layer (receives data), hidden layers (process and find patterns), and an output layer (gives the prediction). Each connection has a weight that is adjusted during training. Deep learning uses many hidden layers — 'deep' refers to the depth of the network. CNNs (Convolutional Neural Networks) excel at image recognition. RNNs/Transformers excel at text and language. Training requires lots of data and computing power (GPUs).
examples: A CNN for image recognition: input image → edges detected → shapes found → object identified
A Transformer for language: processes entire sentences at once to understand context and meaning
Training GPT-like models requires thousands of GPUs running for weeks on billions of text samples

keyTerms.neural network: A computing system of connected nodes organized in layers that learns patterns
keyTerms.deep learning: Neural networks with many hidden layers, capable of learning complex patterns
keyTerms.CNN: Convolutional Neural Network — specialized for processing images and visual data

quiz.question: What makes deep learning 'deep'?
options: Many hidden layers in the neural network
It runs for a long time
quiz.explanation: Deep = many layers between input and output, enabling complex pattern learning.

quiz.question: Which neural network type is best for images?
quiz.explanation: CNNs are designed to process visual data, detecting edges, shapes, and objects.

quiz.question: What are 'weights' in a neural network?
options: Numbers on connections that are adjusted during training
The physical weight of the computer
quiz.explanation: Weights determine how much influence each connection has — training adjusts them for accuracy.

lessons.title: Bias in AI
lessons.content: AI can be biased — it reflects the biases in its training data. If a hiring AI is trained on historical data where most managers were male, it may learn to prefer male candidates. If a facial recognition system is trained mostly on light-skinned faces, it performs worse on dark-skinned faces. Bias can cause real harm: unfair loan denials, wrongful arrests, discriminatory hiring. To fight bias: use diverse training data, test across demographic groups, have diverse development teams, and audit AI systems regularly. AI fairness is an active research area.
examples: Amazon scrapped an AI hiring tool that was biased against women — trained on 10 years of male-dominated resumes
Facial recognition studies showed higher error rates for darker-skinned women compared to lighter-skinned men
A healthcare algorithm gave lower risk scores to Black patients, resulting in less care — it used cost as a proxy for health needs

keyTerms.AI bias: When AI systems produce unfair results due to biased training data or design
keyTerms.fairness: Ensuring AI treats all demographic groups equitably
keyTerms.audit: Systematically checking an AI system for bias and errors

quiz.question: Where does AI bias mainly come from?
quiz.explanation: AI learns from data — if the data reflects historical biases, the AI will too.

quiz.question: How can we reduce AI bias?
options: Use diverse data and test across demographic groups
quiz.explanation: Diverse data, demographic testing, and regular audits help identify and reduce bias.

quiz.question: Why is AI bias harmful?
options: It can lead to unfair discrimination in real decisions
quiz.explanation: Biased AI can deny loans, jobs, or healthcare unfairly based on race, gender, or other factors.

lessons.title: Privacy and Data Ethics
lessons.content: AI needs data, but collecting personal data raises ethical concerns. Privacy: people should know what data is collected and how it's used. Consent: users should agree before their data is used. Data protection laws (GDPR in Europe, POPIA in South Africa) give people rights over their data: access it, correct it, delete it. Surveillance AI (facial recognition in public spaces) raises freedom concerns. Deepfakes use AI to create fake but realistic videos and audio — potential for misinformation and fraud. Responsible AI development means balancing innovation with protecting people's rights.
examples: GDPR requires websites to ask permission before tracking users with cookies
A deepfake video of a politician saying things they never said could influence elections
A health app collecting location data without telling users violates privacy principles

keyTerms.privacy: The right to control what personal information is collected and how it's used
keyTerms.consent: Getting permission from individuals before collecting or using their data
keyTerms.deepfake: AI-generated fake video or audio that looks and sounds realistic

quiz.question: What is GDPR?
options: A European data protection law giving people rights over their data
quiz.explanation: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) protects personal data rights in Europe.

quiz.question: What is a deepfake?
options: AI-generated fake video or audio that looks real
quiz.explanation: Deepfakes use AI to create realistic but fabricated video/audio of real people.

quiz.question: Why is data consent important?
options: People have the right to decide how their data is used
quiz.explanation: Consent respects individual autonomy — people should choose whether to share their data.

lessons.title: The Future of AI
lessons.content: AI is advancing rapidly. Key trends: AI in healthcare (drug discovery, early disease detection), AI for climate (optimizing energy use, predicting weather), AI in education (personalized learning for every student), and AI creativity (generating art, music, and text). Jobs will change: some will be automated, but new ones will emerge (AI trainers, ethicists, data annotators). AI won't replace humans — it will augment human capabilities. The most valuable skill will be knowing how to work WITH AI. Concerns include job displacement, autonomous weapons, and concentration of power in companies that control AI. The future depends on the choices we make today about how to develop and regulate AI.
examples: AlphaFold predicted the structure of nearly every known protein — a breakthrough for drug development
AI-powered tutors could give every child access to personalized education regardless of location
Self-driving trucks may displace millions of truck drivers — society needs retraining programs

keyTerms.augmentation: AI enhancing human abilities rather than replacing humans
keyTerms.automation: Using AI/machines to perform tasks previously done by humans
keyTerms.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence — hypothetical AI matching human intelligence across all domains

quiz.question: Will AI replace all human jobs?
options: No — it will change some jobs and create new ones
Yes — all jobs will be automated
quiz.explanation: AI will automate some tasks but create new roles — the key is adaptation and retraining.

quiz.question: What is AI augmentation?
options: AI helping humans do their jobs better
quiz.explanation: Augmentation means AI works alongside humans, enhancing their capabilities.

quiz.question: What is the most important skill in an AI-powered future?
options: Knowing how to work with AI effectively
quiz.explanation: Understanding AI and using it as a tool will be essential across all careers.
